title: Thermodynamic efficiency of communication channels
authors: Nahuel Freitas, Pedro E. Harunari, Massimiliano Esposito
abstract: We identify a broad class of communication channels that captures common physical constraints in both artificial and natural systems and derive bounds on their thermodynamic cost. We find that the entropy production per channel use is bounded from below by the input-output mutual information, and their ratio -mutual information divided by entropy production- defines the thermodynamic efficiency. Unlike previous studies of energy-constrained communication channels, our analysis shows that thermodynamic costs must be assigned not only to the input symbols themselves, but also to transitions between successive symbols. As a result, maximizing thermodynamic efficiency favors a biased input that switches only rarely, rather than the capacity-achieving input. For the binary symmetric channel, this preference emerges through a pitchfork bifurcation that spontaneously breaks the symmetry of the channel. A minimal model of cellular sensing exhibits the same phenomenon.
summary: This work establishes a thermodynamic efficiency measure for communication channels by bounding the entropy production cost. It shows that optimizing this efficiency favors biased inputs that minimize costly state transitions, rather than maximizing raw information capacity. This has implications for understanding energy dissipation in natural and artificial information processing systems.
main_problem: The paper derives bounds on the thermodynamic cost (entropy production) associated with communication channels and defines a thermodynamic efficiency metric.
main_result: The thermodynamic efficiency is bounded by unity, and maximizing it favors a biased input that switches rarely, leading to spontaneous symmetry breaking in simple models.
method: The analysis uses information theory concepts (mutual information, capacity) combined with non-equilibrium thermodynamics, decomposing entropy production into adiabatic and non-adiabatic parts.
model_or_system: The study applies to a general class of communication channels relevant to both artificial and natural systems, exemplified by the Binary Symmetric Channel (BSC) and a minimal cellular sensing model.
key_observables: Mutual Information ($I$), Channel Capacity ($C$), Entropy Production ($\Sigma$), and Thermodynamic Efficiency ($\eta = I/\Sigma$).
important_parameters: Input bias parameter ($b$), channel error rate ($\epsilon$), and the ratio of transition to idle entropy production ($r$).
main_assumptions: The analysis assumes specific time-scale separations and that the cost must account for transitions between successive symbols, not just the input symbols themselves.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate the dependence of efficiency ($\eta$) on input bias ($b$) and show the non-trivial symmetry breaking transition in the BSC case.
paper_structure: The paper establishes the fundamental thermodynamic bound ($k_b I \le \Sigma_s$), defines efficiency, and then applies this framework to specific models like the BSC, demonstrating how optimization leads to biased, symmetry-breaking inputs.
why_interesting: The focus on non-equilibrium thermodynamics, entropy production bounds, and the interplay between information capacity and thermodynamic cost is highly relevant to open quantum systems and quantum thermodynamics.
